title: Privacy | Museum of Ages, a digital museum
description: How Museum of Ages, a digital museum, handles data: no account, no cookies of ours, what we count ourselves, and what the host and your browser do.
lead: This page says what happens to data when you visit Museum of Ages. In short: you need no account, we set no cookies, and we keep nothing that lets us recognise you on your next visit.

body: Museum of Ages is run by ChipMates gemeinnützige GmbH, Schusterstr. 50, 79098 Freiburg im Breisgau, Germany. You reach us at [contact@museumofages.org](mailto:contact@museumofages.org). The full details are in the [legal notice](page:imprint).
We have not appointed a data protection officer, because the law does not require one for us (Art. 37 GDPR and § 38 BDSG, the German Federal Data Protection Act).

To show you a page, your browser asks our host for it. The host's servers then process your IP address, the address of the page, the date and time, and what your browser says about itself, such as which browser it is, its language and the page you came from. Without your IP address no page can reach you. The other details your browser sends along with every request.

Our host is Cloudflare, Inc., 101 Townsend St, San Francisco, CA 94107, USA. Cloudflare delivers this site for us under a data processing agreement. To protect its own network, Cloudflare also evaluates connection data on its own responsibility, as its privacy policy describes.
The legal basis is Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR. Our legitimate interest is to deliver the site reliably and to protect it against attacks.

We keep no server logs of our own. Cloudflare keeps the request records it shows us for up to 31 days. For its own logs, [Cloudflare's privacy policy](https://www.cloudflare.com/privacypolicy/) names the rules it deletes by and no fixed number of days.

Cloudflare shows us totals for the site: how many requests arrived, for which pages, and how much data they moved, about how many different visitors there were, from which countries the requests came, and how many Cloudflare stopped. These totals name no one.

Cloudflare also shows us a sample of single requests from the last 31 days. Each one has its IP address, the address of the page, the country and the name of the browser. The sample holds requests Cloudflare let through as well as those it stopped or checked. We use it to find attacks and faults.
This site shows no advertising and loads no analytics tools, counting pixels or scripts from other companies. What we count ourselves is in the next section.

We count how the museum is used ourselves, without cookies and without recognising anyone. When one of the steps below happens, the page sends a short count to an address of this site's own, at the same host, into a datastore of our own. Cloudflare runs it for us, under the data processing agreement. Each count becomes one row there. Nothing goes to any other provider. The page does not read what the server answers.

In the wing there are four steps. The arrival: a wing is opened. A stop: you reach one. A close look: you look closer at a work. The use: a visit was more than a glance, that is, you reach the second stop or open the first close look. Each row holds which wing it was, which language the wing is showing, and how the screen stood: upright, sideways or wide. A stop adds its number (1 to 17), a close look adds the kind of work: painting, machine, sheet, book, film or place, never which work. The arrival and the use also carry the source word that the next section explains.

On the site's pages there are three steps: a page is opened. The middle of its text comes into view. A link into the wing is pressed. Each row holds which page it is, from a fixed list (the home page, the page on Leonardo, the inventions, "What this museum is", privacy, the legal notice, and each page that is added), and which language the page is showing. Opening adds whether the visit began on this page, and if so, the source word. The link adds where it stood on the page: at the top, at an entry or at the end.

The server adds two details to each row: the country as a two-letter code that Cloudflare derives from the connection, and a device class, phone, tablet or desktop, worked out from what your browser says about itself. It keeps neither your IP address nor what your browser said. The moment a row was written is stamped by the datastore itself.

Each step counts at most once per page load: a wing once, each stop once, each work once, a page once. The page remembers this only while it is open and writes nothing to your browser for it. If you reload it, it counts again. No row carries an identifier or an IP address. We do not join rows with each other or with other data, and we only read totals. If a detail is not on its fixed list, that detail or the whole row is dropped. The datastore deletes the rows by itself after three months. Totals we make from them hold no single row.

For the counting, nothing is stored on your device and nothing stored there is read. The one exception is a mark meant for our own test browsers, described under "Cookies and storage in your browser". That is why we do not ask for consent for the counting (§ 25 TDDDG, the German law on data protection in digital services). The legal basis is Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR. Our legitimate interest is to know whether the museum is used and whom it reaches.

When a visit begins, the count notes in one coarse word what kind of place it came from. The word comes from a fixed list of fifteen, and all visits of the same kind get the same word: "direct" (no linking page), "search" (a search engine), "ad through Google's program for nonprofits", "paid ad", "paid ad in a forum", "forum", "code platform", "educational institution", "wiki", "news site", "e-mail", "award" (the site of a prize or a gallery), "AI assistant", "social network or messenger" and "other website" (any other linking site). It sits on the row for the page where the visit began, and in the wing on the rows for the arrival and the use. Only that word is kept.
It is worked out once, when the visit begins, in this order:
Links we place ourselves, for example in an ad or under a post of our own in a forum, have an address of their own on this site. That is how the count knows an ad or a post brought the visit.

If you go from one of our pages into the wing, and the visit began on that page, the page passes its word along with the link, at the end of the address after the hash sign. The wing reads it once and stores nothing.

For every other visit, the word is worked out as the page is delivered, on the server, from the detail of which page you came from. Your browser sends that with its request by itself, as described above under "When you open a page". The page reaches you with that one word. No script looks up in your browser where you came from. If the detail is missing, the word is "direct". If you come from another page of this site, the visit did not begin here, and the row gets no word.

For the counting, we never read, store or send what stands after the question mark of an address, the part where services attach extras to a link. The exceptions are the extra probe=1 for our test browsers and the language the wing takes from its own address. If an ad platform attaches a click number to its link, the count never takes it in. The count keeps no full address of the linking page, no name of its host and no search words.

sections.h: Cookies and storage in your browser
body: We set no cookies. The pages of this site store nothing in your browser, with one exception that is meant for our own test browsers and is in the list below. One case is the host's: if Cloudflare's protection checks your browser before it lets a request through, Cloudflare sets a cookie named cf_clearance so that it does not check you again at once. The cookie serves only that.
The wing you walk through keeps a few short notes in your browser's storage so that it works the way you left it. To these comes the mark of our test browsers:
Your sound setting, on or off, and your walking pace if you chose one.
Your language, if you chose one in the wing.
A mark that your device gets one scene as a film. It is set once if the device is too slow for the live scene.
For the open tab only: that the opening and a hint have already been shown, and a time mark if the wing had to reload once after a graphics error.

A mark meant only for our own test browsers. It is set when an address of this site is opened with the extra ?probe=1. The count reads only this one mark from storage and notes on its rows that it is there, so that we can take our own visits out. If you set it yourself, we take your visits out like ours.

These notes stay on your device until you clear them. The notes for the open tab go when you close it. None of the wing's notes is sent to us or to anyone else. Of the test browsers' mark, only that it is there is noted. You remove all of it by clearing this site's data in your browser.

We do not ask for consent for these notes, because they are needed for a function you use (§ 25 (2) no. 2 TDDDG). The same rule covers the host's cookie: without it a checked browser would be checked again on every page. The test browsers' mark is meant only for our own devices. On yours the count finds nothing, unless you set it yourself.
Fonts, pictures, films and scripts come from this site and from our own storage at the same host. The pages load no fonts, maps, videos or buttons from other companies.

Some pages link to other websites, for example to the museums, libraries and collections that hold the originals, and to our source code. When you follow such a link, you leave this site and the other site's rules apply.

sections.h: When you write to us or call us
body: If you send us an e-mail or call us, we use your address or number and what you tell us to answer you. The legal basis is Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR, our legitimate interest in answering. Our e-mail runs with a mail provider in Switzerland that handles it on our behalf. The European Commission has recognised Switzerland as a country with adequate data protection. We delete the exchange when the matter is closed, unless the law obliges us to keep it longer.

Cloudflare is a company in the USA and answers requests from servers around the world, as a rule from one near you. For transfers to the USA, Cloudflare is certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, which the European Commission recognised as adequate protection on 10 July 2023. Our agreement with Cloudflare also contains the EU's standard contractual clauses, for any transfer the framework does not cover. The agreement is public: [Cloudflare's data processing addendum](https://www.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-customer-dpa/).

Under the GDPR you have the right to learn which data about you we process (Art. 15), to have wrong data corrected (Art. 16), to have data erased (Art. 17), to have its processing restricted (Art. 18) and, where the law grants it, to receive data you gave us in a common format (Art. 20).

You can also complain to a data protection authority (Art. 77). The one responsible for us is the Landesbeauftragte für den Datenschutz und die Informationsfreiheit Baden-Württemberg, Heilbronner Straße 35, 70191 Stuttgart, [www.baden-wuerttemberg.datenschutz.de](https://www.baden-wuerttemberg.datenschutz.de).

To be plain about it: we hold almost nothing that we could look up for you. There are no accounts, the wing's notes are on your device, not with us, and the count carries no identifier by which we could find your rows.
We make no automated decisions about you and build no profiles.
You can object at any time, for reasons that arise from your particular situation, to processing that rests on our legitimate interest (Art. 21 GDPR). Write to the address at the top of this page.

You can also object to the count without writing to us: if your browser sends the Global Privacy Control signal, the count writes no row for it. Some browsers send it on their own, others let you turn it on in their settings or with an extension.
This page describes the site as it is today. If something changes, this page is changed first.
